title: the summit sit
hook: palm leaves in a locked room, a clay goddess going back to the river, sandals in a palanquin: what each region carries

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit went back to the women in their own words, and the names they signed: Mira's Lord is Giridhar. Did you notice whose words you were carrying when you signed your name? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.

Palm leaves in a locked temple room, half eaten by ants. A goddess shaped from river clay, welcomed home like a daughter and then carried back to the water. A silver palanquin in a sea of white caps, and inside it, a pair of sandals. A cloth bundle on a pilgrim's head. Walnuts soaked through the night and handed to the neighbors. Those are things this year held in its hands, one region at a time. Today is the last of the summit sits, and it goes back to the regional traditions, to see what each place carries.
screen: `PALM LEAVES AND RIVER CLAY.` → `SANDALS IN A PALANQUIN.` → `WHAT EACH PLACE CARRIES.`

segments.voice: Walk the map again, one object at a time. In Tamil country, the story of the Tevaram: palm leaves found in a locked room, much of them eaten away, and a voice saying what this age needs has been kept. In Bengal, Durga in clay, who is also Uma, a daughter come home to her worried mother, and sent back to the river when the festival ends. In Maharashtra, the Varkaris walking to Pandharpur with the sandals of their saints, because the sandals stand for the one who walked in them. In Kashmir, pots of water and walnuts kept through Shiva's great night, and the walnuts shared out the next day. In Kerala, the bundle on the pilgrim's head on the climb to Sabarimala: offerings in one part, food for the road in the other. In Gujarat, a letter of daily conduct, written by a teacher for people he would never meet. In Punjab, a song by Namdev, a tailor from Maharashtra, kept in the Sikh scripture, about a boy whose mind stays on his kite string. Now turn it. Each of these belongs to its own place, its own language, its own community, and this year let each one speak in its own words. They aren't lined up from lesser to greater. They aren't melted into one. And still, look at what the objects do. Almost every one of them is carried, handed on, or shared. Leaves kept, a daughter sent off, sandals borne along a road, a bundle on a head, walnuts given next door, a letter sent ahead, a song that traveled north. A tradition that lives in many places lives, in part, by things passed from hand to hand.
screen: `TAMIL PALM LEAVES, BENGALI CLAY.` · `SANDALS, WALNUTS, A BUNDLE, A LETTER.` · `EACH IN ITS OWN WORDS, NONE RANKED.` · `PASSED FROM HAND TO HAND.` · then, large: `WHAT EACH PLACE CARRIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: what was handed on. Sit, and let the breath find its pace. Bring to mind one thing that was handed to you: a recipe, a song, a name, a habit, a pair of old shoes. Don't judge its worth. Picture the person who handed it to you, and, if you can, whoever handed it to them. Stay with that short chain for a few breaths. Then think of someone you might hand something to, one day. If you pray, you can offer that thing, and that person, to God in your own way. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch, and the last: the regional traditions, and what each place carries. Today's word.

Your line: the summit sit. Today, hand one small thing on: a dish, a song, a kind word, the way the walnuts went next door. Tomorrow, the whole year, looked at from the top. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Regional festivals and pilgrimages such as Durga Puja in Bengal, the Pandharpur wari in Maharashtra, Herath in Kashmir and the Sabarimala pilgrimage in Kerala are kept by families and communities in their own languages and customs.

fork.setup: you're on the climb to Sabarimala with a cloth bundle on your head. it's tied in two parts. what's in them?
options: offerings for the god, and food for the road.
nothing; the bundle is a symbol.
fork.reveal: one part carries offerings, including a coconut filled with ghee; the other carries food for the road.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: svāmī, master or lord; on the Sabarimala path, the name pilgrims call one another.

trapdoor: what you thought: the regional traditions are local versions of one Hinduism.
what it means: each belongs to its own place and language, taught in its own words, none ranked.

what a scholar hears: Tamil Shaiva, Bengali Shakta and Vaishnava, Varkari, Kashmiri, Keralan and Swaminarayan traditions, each with its own texts, saints and festivals, here read side by side through things carried and shared.

notes: Last summit sit (1412–1424): revisits 'Regional traditions' (1370–1411). Recaps follow the year's scripts: Tevaram 1370, Durga/Uma 1379, padukas 1385, Herath 1393, Sabarimala 1399, the Swaminarayan letter of conduct 1403, Namdev's kite 1406.
'A short letter of daily conduct' is taken to be the Shikshapatri, per the hook of 1403; confirm.
The Ang number for Namdev's kite hymn (972) should be checked against day 1406's sources before release; it is in sources only, not spoken.
'Almost every one of them is carried, handed on, or shared' is this script's own observation about the objects chosen, not a claim about the traditions; a Keeper may want it softened.
Tevaram story given as 'the story' (tradition), not history. Original: स्वामी (svāmī) as the name pilgrims call each other on the Sabarimala path, per 1399; confirm.
